**Voices in the Dark: Building the Clandestine Radio**

*Gallery 4 — The Resistance at Home*

When nations fell to German occupation in 1940, the resistance needed a voice — and the enemy knew it. Radio transmitters were contraband of the highest order: possessing one could mean torture and death. So resistance networks built their own, by hand, in cellars and attics.

**Scavenged and improvised.** With commercial components unobtainable, builders raided what was at hand. Coils were wound from enameled wire stripped from motors or salvaged from wrecked vehicles. Capacitors came from discarded radios; mica sheets were cut from window glass substitutes. Some circuits used graphite pencil marks on paper as resistors.

**Miniaturization as survival.** Early sets filled suitcases. As detection vans — the *Funkpeilwagen* — prowled cities triangulating illegal transmissions, transmitters shrank. By 1943, skilled builders like the Dutch and Belgian *pia* (parachutists' radio operators) carried sets small enough to fit in a biscuit tin, powered by bicycle dynamos or hand-cranked generators, transmitting in bursts of seconds before vanishing.

**The operator's craft.** A set was only half the story. Operators memorized cipher keys, changed frequencies on rigid schedules (*quarts*), and transmitted from a different window or rooftop each night — moving before the direction-finding vans could close in. A transmission lasting more than a few minutes could be fatal.

**The cost.** Thousands of operators were caught. But by 1944, hundreds of clandestine stations were reporting troop movements, guiding supply drops, and coordinating with London. Many of the sets displayed here were recovered from hiding places after liberation — some still holding the last message their operator sent.

*On display: a "suitcase set" B Mk II (British SOE issue), a locally built Belgian transmitter recovered from a chimney cavity, and a hand-crank generator used by the Polish Home Army.*
